```{python}
#| label: setup
#| include: false
import pandas as pd
import numpy as np
import plotly.express as px
import plotly.graph_objects as go
from collections import defaultdict
from pathlib import Path

ROOT = Path(".").resolve()
scored = pd.read_parquet(ROOT / "clues_scored.parquet")
labels = (pd.read_csv(ROOT.parent / "jeopardy_ds" / "cluster_labels.csv")
            .set_index("cluster_id")["name"].to_dict())

board = scored[
    (scored["media"] == False) &
    (scored["game_type"] == "regular") &
    (scored["round"].isin(["Jeopardy", "Double Jeopardy"])) &
    (scored["is_daily_double"] == False) &
    scored["difficulty"].notna() &
    ((scored["n_right"] > 0) | (scored["n_wrong"] > 0) | scored["is_triple_stumper"])
].copy()

board["any_correct"] = (board["n_right"] > 0).astype(float)
board["year"] = board["air_date"].dt.year
board["adj_row"] = board["row"]
board["round_num"] = board["round"].map({"Jeopardy": 0, "Double Jeopardy": 1})

train = board[~board["in_test_game"] & ~board["in_spike_game"]]
test  = board[board["in_test_game"]]
```

## Introduction

The Jeopardy board looks like a difficulty ladder: cheapest clue in the top-left corner, most expensive in the bottom-right. But anyone who watches regularly knows that's a lie. The $200 clue about Baroque composers can stump three strong players while the $2,000 clue about a pop star that everyone knows gets buzzed in before Alex finishes reading it.

So what actually makes a Jeopardy clue hard?

I scored every text clue in the J-Archive dataset — around 500,000 of them — using [Jev](https://typesafe.ai/blog/introducing-system-one-models-and-jev), a structured-output model from TypeSafe AI that returns a difficulty integer (1–10) and a calibrated confidence score. Then I compared its ratings against real player outcomes: which clues got answered, which ones stumped everyone, and which ones nobody even attempted (Triple Stumpers).

The headline question: **does the AI's difficulty score predict who gets it right better than dollar value alone?**

To find out, I split the dataset by game, trained a simple lookup-table model on most games, and compared its Brier score on held-out test games with and without the Jev difficulty score added in. The Brier score measures calibration — how far off your probability estimates are from the true 0/1 outcomes.

Here are three clues that make the problem vivid:

```{python}
#| label: intro-examples
#| echo: false
cheap_stumpers = board[(board["clue_value"] <= 400) & board["is_triple_stumper"]].nlargest(3, "difficulty")
easy_expensive = board[(board["clue_value"] >= 1600) & (board["n_right"] > 0)].nsmallest(3, "difficulty")
jev_wrong = board[(board["difficulty"] <= 3) & board["is_triple_stumper"]].head(3)

print("Cheap clues that stumped everyone (high AI difficulty, low dollar value):")
print(cheap_stumpers[["category", "clue", "answer", "clue_value", "difficulty"]].to_string(index=False))
print("\nExpensive clues everyone answered (low AI difficulty, high dollar value):")
print(easy_expensive[["category", "clue", "answer", "clue_value", "difficulty"]].to_string(index=False))
print("\nClues the AI rated easy that still stumped everyone:")
print(jev_wrong[["category", "clue", "answer", "difficulty"]].to_string(index=False))
```

## Analysis

### Dollar value vs correctness

First, let's confirm the baseline: does board position actually predict player success?

```{python}
#| label: fig-baseline
#| fig-cap: "Mean fraction of correct responses by row position (1=cheapest, 5=most expensive). Aggregated across Jeopardy and Double Jeopardy board clues."
baseline = board.groupby("adj_row")["any_correct"].mean().reset_index()
fig = px.bar(baseline, x="adj_row", y="any_correct",
             labels={"adj_row": "Row (1=cheapest, 5=most expensive)",
                     "any_correct": "Fraction answered correctly"},
             title="Dollar value predicts correctness — but imperfectly")
fig.update_layout(margin={"t": 50})
fig.show()
```

### Jev difficulty vs correctness

Now the key question: does the AI's difficulty rating track with actual player performance?

```{python}
#| label: fig-jev-vs-correct
#| fig-cap: "Mean fraction correct by Jev difficulty bucket (1–10), with a linear trend."
bucket_corr = board.groupby("difficulty")["any_correct"].mean().reset_index()
m, b = np.polyfit(bucket_corr["difficulty"], bucket_corr["any_correct"], 1)
bucket_corr["trend"] = m * bucket_corr["difficulty"] + b
fig = go.Figure()
fig.add_trace(go.Scatter(x=bucket_corr["difficulty"], y=bucket_corr["any_correct"],
                         mode="markers+text", name="Mean fraction correct",
                         text=bucket_corr["difficulty"].astype(str),
                         textposition="top center"))
fig.add_trace(go.Scatter(x=bucket_corr["difficulty"], y=bucket_corr["trend"],
                         mode="lines", name="Linear trend", line={"dash": "dot"}))
fig.update_layout(title="Jev difficulty vs fraction of clues answered correctly",
                  xaxis_title="Jev difficulty (1–10)",
                  yaxis_title="Fraction answered correctly",
                  margin={"t": 50})
fig.show()
```

### Validation: does Jev beat dollar value?

The real test. I split the games into training and test sets (20% held out, pre-selected before any prompt development). Two models:

- **Baseline:** lookup `P(any_correct | row, round)` from training data
- **Full model:** lookup `P(any_correct | row, round, difficulty)` from training data

Brier score on the held-out test games, with 95% bootstrap confidence intervals (bootstrap by game to preserve the natural clustering of clues within games).

```{python}
#| label: fig-brier
#| fig-cap: "Brier score (lower = better) for the baseline model (row + round) and the full model (row + round + Jev difficulty). The improvement and 95% CI are reported above the chart."
train_means = train.groupby(["adj_row", "round_num"])["any_correct"].mean()
def predict_baseline(df):
    return df.set_index(["adj_row", "round_num"]).index.map(
        lambda k: train_means.get(k, train_means.mean()))

train_means_full = train.groupby(["adj_row", "round_num", "difficulty"])["any_correct"].mean()
def predict_full(df):
    return df.set_index(["adj_row", "round_num", "difficulty"]).index.map(
        lambda k: train_means_full.get(k, train_means.get(k[:2], train_means.mean())))

y_true = test["any_correct"].values
baseline_pred = np.array(predict_baseline(test[["adj_row", "round_num"]]))
full_pred = np.array(predict_full(test[["adj_row", "round_num", "difficulty"]]))

def brier(y, yhat): return np.mean((yhat - y) ** 2)

rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
game_ids = test["game_id"].unique()
game_to_idx = defaultdict(list)
for pos, gid in enumerate(test["game_id"]):
    game_to_idx[gid].append(pos)
boot_diff = []
for _ in range(500):
    sampled_games = rng.choice(game_ids, size=len(game_ids), replace=True)
    boot_idx = np.concatenate([game_to_idx[gid] for gid in sampled_games])
    boot_diff.append(brier(y_true[boot_idx], baseline_pred[boot_idx]) -
                     brier(y_true[boot_idx], full_pred[boot_idx]))
improvement = brier(y_true, baseline_pred) - brier(y_true, full_pred)
ci_lo, ci_hi = np.percentile(boot_diff, [2.5, 97.5])
print(f"Brier improvement (baseline → +Jev): {improvement:.4f} [95% CI: {ci_lo:.4f}, {ci_hi:.4f}]")

fig = px.bar(
    x=["Baseline (row + round)", "Baseline + Jev difficulty"],
    y=[brier(y_true, baseline_pred), brier(y_true, full_pred)],
    labels={"x": "", "y": "Brier score (lower = better)"},
    title="Brier score: baseline vs. baseline + Jev difficulty",
    color_discrete_sequence=["#636efa", "#00cc96"],
)
fig.update_layout(showlegend=False, margin={"t": 50})
fig.show()
```

### Has the show gotten harder over time?

```{python}
#| label: fig-yearly
#| fig-cap: "Mean Jev difficulty score by year. Post-2001 values use the doubled dollar values introduced that year."
yearly = board.groupby("year")["difficulty"].mean().reset_index()
fig = px.line(yearly, x="year", y="difficulty",
              title="Mean Jev difficulty over time",
              labels={"year": "Year", "difficulty": "Mean difficulty (1–10)"})
fig.update_layout(margin={"t": 50})
fig.show()
```

### Difficulty by game type

```{python}
#| label: fig-game-type
#| fig-cap: "Fraction of clues at each Jev difficulty level (1–10), broken out by game type."
agg = (scored[scored["difficulty"].notna()]
       .groupby(["game_type", "difficulty"])
       .size().reset_index(name="count"))
agg["pct"] = agg["count"] / agg.groupby("game_type")["count"].transform("sum")
fig = px.bar(agg, x="difficulty", y="pct", color="game_type", barmode="group",
             title="Difficulty distribution by game type",
             labels={"difficulty": "Jev difficulty (1–10)", "pct": "Fraction of clues",
                     "game_type": "Game type"})
fig.update_layout(margin={"t": 50})
fig.show()
```

### Difficulty by category type

Categories cluster into recognizable types — for details on the clustering methodology, see the [companion post](../jeopardy_ds/). Here are the 20 most common category types ranked by mean difficulty.

```{python}
#| label: fig-clusters
#| fig-cap: "Mean Jev difficulty for the 20 most common category types, ranked by volume."
clusters_raw = pd.read_parquet(ROOT.parent / "jeopardy_ds" / "category_clusters.parquet")
board_with_cluster = board.merge(
    clusters_raw[["game_id", "round", "category", "cluster_id"]],
    on=["game_id", "round", "category"], how="left"
)
board_with_cluster["cluster_name"] = board_with_cluster["cluster_id"].map(labels).fillna("Misc")
cluster_diff = (board_with_cluster.groupby("cluster_name")["difficulty"]
                .agg(["mean", "count"]).reset_index()
                .sort_values("count", ascending=False).head(20)
                .sort_values("mean"))
fig = px.bar(cluster_diff, x="mean", y="cluster_name", orientation="h",
             title="Mean difficulty by category cluster (top 20 by volume)",
             labels={"mean": "Mean Jev difficulty", "cluster_name": ""})
fig.update_layout(height=550, margin={"t": 50, "l": 200})
fig.show()
```

## How the prompt was developed

Finding a rubric that reliably produces well-calibrated 1–10 ratings required some experimentation. Jev doesn't take a freeform prompt — it takes structured questions, with a rubric of descriptions for each score level. The framing of those descriptions turned out to matter a lot.

I sampled 500 clues stratified by board position and scored them with three different rubric formulations, all using the same instruction ("You are an expert Jeopardy analyst. Rate how difficult this clue is for a typical contestant.") but varying the per-level descriptions. I selected the winner on two criteria: strongest negative correlation with actual player correctness, and median difficulty close to 5 (a well-centered scale is more interpretable and suggests the model isn't systematically over- or under-estimating).

| Variant | Description style | Corr | Median |
|---|---|---|---|
| Descriptive | Narrative anchors ("almost anyone would know this…") | -0.182 | 5.0 |
| **Percentile** | **Player correctness rates ("~45% of contestants answer correctly")** | **-0.227** | **5.0** |
| Concise | Short labels ("median — typical for a Jeopardy contestant") | -0.191 | 4.0 |

The percentile variant won on both axes. Grounding each level in a concrete expected correctness rate gives Jev a clear, measurable signal to anchor its judgment — rather than asking it to interpret vague qualitative labels like "somewhat easy."

The spike sample was carved out *before* any rubric development, and those games are excluded from the training set used in the validation above — so rubric selection can't leak into the test result.
